subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.activity_title: Counting Squares: Rebuilding the Rectangle Area Formula

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.1 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Think of different creative ways to divide a square into 4 parts of equal area using compression and expansion along edges.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the missing side-lengths of composite rectangular figures given their areas: (i) an L-shaped figure with partial lengths 4 in, 3 in, 7 in, 2 in and areas 28 in² and 21 in²; (ii) a rectangle with one side 4 m, one side 11 m, and total area 50 m².

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.1 p.152
homework.description: A square is divided into three regions (1, 2, 3). If the side-length is doubled, find the increase in the areas of regions 1, 2, and 3. Give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Students draw rectangles of various sizes on squared paper and count unit squares to confirm the area. The teacher elicits the generalisation: area of a rectangle = length × width.

Math Talk, section 7.1 p.148 (“Think of different creative ways to divide a square into 4 parts of equal area…”): pairs sketch as many dissections as possible, then share. The class observes that equal-area parts need not be congruent.

Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 (“Identify the missing side-lengths of composite rectangular figures…”): students use the rectangle formula in reverse, working from given areas to unknown side-lengths for the L-shape and the plain rectangle.
Whole-class debrief: students explain their reverse-computation strategy aloud. The teacher records the two-step method — area ÷ known side = unknown side — on the board as a class-derived rule.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who multiply all three visible dimensions of the L-shape instead of splitting it into two rectangles; prompt them to draw the dividing line first. The reverse-computation step — given area, find a side — is the conceptual pivot of this unit, so press students to articulate it in their own words before moving on.

periods.activity_title: Same Perimeter, Different Area: Reasoning Through the Gap

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.151
textbook_items_in_class.description: A shaded path is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a larger rectangle ABCD. (i) Assign measurements of your choice and find the area of the path; give a formula. (ii) If the path width along each side is given, find its area by breaking into rectangles; give a formula. (iii) Determine whether the path area changes when the outer rectangle is shifted while keeping EFGH inside.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q3, section 7.1 p.151
textbook_items_in_class.description: A plot of 14 m × 12 m has a crosspath. Identify necessary measurements, assign values, find the area of the crosspath, and give a formula.

homework.description: Divide a square into 4 parts by drawing two perpendicular lines inside it, then rearrange the pieces to form a larger square with a hole inside. Try using cardboard cut-outs.

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses a quick challenge: draw two rectangles each with perimeter 20 cm but different areas. Students share their examples, building the central insight that perimeter alone does not determine area.

Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.151 (“A shaded path is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a larger rectangle ABCD…”): small groups assign their own measurements, compute path area by subtraction, then derive a general formula. Part (iii) — does shifting the outer rectangle change the path area? — drives the reasoning discussion.

Math Talk Q3, section 7.1 p.151 (“A plot of 14 m × 12 m has a crosspath…”): students identify which measurements are needed, assign values, compute the crosspath area (with the overlap square corrected), and write a general formula.

Groups share their crosspath formulas. The teacher highlights the inclusion-exclusion correction — subtracting the central overlapping square — and connects it to the perimeter-vs-area independence reasoning from the opening challenge.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in the crosspath problem is adding the two strips without subtracting the central square counted twice; draw attention to this overlap explicitly. The path-area problem (Q2 part iii) is the deeper reasoning item — encourage students to test with a numerical example before making the general claim.

periods.activity_title: Half the Rectangle: Proving the Triangle Area Formula

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.157
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the areas of three triangles: (i) triangle with base 4 cm and height 3 cm; (ii) triangle ENT with base EN = 4 cm and height 3.2 cm; (iii) triangle ANT with base AT = 3 cm and height from N.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.2 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of isosceles triangle SUB, given that SE ⊥ UB and the area of triangle SEB is 24 sq. units.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.158
homework.description: Find the length of altitude BY in triangle ABC, given base BC = 6 units, altitude AX = 8 units (with foot X on BC), and AC = 4 units.

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a triangle inside its enclosing rectangle and asks: what fraction of the rectangle does the triangle occupy? The class reasons through the acute case — the diagonal splits the rectangle into two congruent triangles — establishing area of triangle = (1/2) × base × height.

The teacher extends the argument to an obtuse triangle whose altitude falls outside the base, showing via the difference-of-two-right-triangles derivation that the formula holds universally. Students sketch both cases and annotate the congruence step.
Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.157 (“Find the areas of three triangles…”): students apply the formula to the three cases, including one where the height is not the side of the triangle.

Figure it Out Q3, section 7.2 p.158 (“Find the area of isosceles triangle SUB, given that SE ⊥ UB…”): students use the symmetry of the isosceles triangle and the given half-area to find the whole area, reinforcing the idea that the altitude can split the triangle into two equal parts.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse a slant side with the height; emphasise that the height is always the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base line, not the slant edge. The obtuse-triangle case — where the foot of the altitude lies outside the base segment — is the most common source of conceptual error and deserves its own annotated sketch on the board.

periods.activity_title: Altitude Hunting and Triangles Between Parallel Lines

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 7.2 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: ABCD, BCEF, and BFGH are three identical squares. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, find the area of the blue region. (ii) If the total area of blue and red regions is 180 sq. units, find the area of each square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q7, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: M and N are the midpoints of XY and XZ respectively. What fraction of the area of triangle XYZ is the area of triangle XMN? [Hint: Join NY.]

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q8, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Gopal must travel from his house to the river and then to his water tank. Find the shortest path using the mirror-reflection principle. Sketch the path on a rough map.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.2 p.158
homework.description: [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a rectangle into a triangle of equal area.

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the result that triangles sharing a common base whose apices lie on a line parallel to the base all have equal area. Students draw three such triangles on grid paper and verify the equal-area claim by computing each.

Figure it Out Q6, section 7.2 p.158 (“ABCD, BCEF, and BFGH are three identical squares…”): students use the parallel-lines equal-area principle and the triangle area formula to relate the red and blue regions across the three squares.

Try This Q7, section 7.2 p.159 (“M and N are the midpoints of XY and XZ…”): students use the hint — join NY — and the equal-area lemma for triangles on parallel lines to establish that triangle XMN is one-quarter of triangle XYZ.

Math Talk Q8, section 7.2 p.159 (“Gopal must travel from his house to the river and then to his water tank…”): students sketch the scenario and apply the mirror-reflection principle to locate the shortest-path apex on the river line, connecting minimum-perimeter reasoning to the triangle area context.

periods.teacher_notes: The midpoint-fraction problem (Q7) is best approached by computing both areas symbolically with a general base and height; students who assign specific numbers sometimes miss the generality of the one-quarter result. For the mirror-reflection problem, watch for students who confuse the shortest path with a perpendicular to the river — the correct path is the one that makes equal angles with the riverbank.

periods.activity_title: Divide and Conquer: Triangle Decomposition of Polygons

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of quadrilateral ABCD given AC = 22 cm, BM ⊥ AC with BM = 3 cm, and DN ⊥ AC with DN = 3 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of the shaded region given that ABCD is a rectangle with dimensions 18 cm × 10 cm and an interior quadrilateral AEFB is cut out, with AE = 10 cm, EF = 4 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q3, section 7.3 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: What measurements would you need to find the area of a regular hexagon?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q4, section 7.3 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: What fraction of the total area of a rectangle is the area of the blue region (a triangle formed by connecting specific vertices)?

homework.description: Give a method to obtain a quadrilateral whose area is half that of a given quadrilateral.

time_bands.activity: Students draw any quadrilateral on plain paper and then draw one diagonal. The teacher asks: how many triangles appear, and what do you know about each one? The class agrees on the decomposition strategy: area of polygon = sum of triangle areas.

Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.160 (“Find the area of quadrilateral ABCD given AC = 22 cm…”): students use diagonal AC as the shared base of two triangles, applying the triangle area formula with perpendicular heights BM and DN.

Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.160 (“Find the area of the shaded region given that ABCD is a rectangle…”): students decompose the interior quadrilateral AEFB into triangles, compute its area, and subtract from the rectangle area to find the shaded region.

Math Talk Q3, section 7.3 p.160 (“What measurements would you need to find the area of a regular hexagon?”) and Math Talk Q4, section 7.3 p.160 (“What fraction of the total area of a rectangle is the area of the blue region?”): groups discuss and report, extending the decomposition strategy to regular polygons and fraction reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight here is that any polygon's area becomes computable once it is decomposed into triangles; watch for students who try to use the perimeter or count only some of the triangles. For Q1, students sometimes add both heights to the same triangle rather than assigning each perpendicular to its correct triangle — a quick sketch with labelled triangles prevents this.

periods.activity_title: Cut and Slide: Deriving the Parallelogram Area by Dissection

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (parallelogram dissection), section 7.4 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using a cut-out of a parallelogram, convert it into a rectangle of equal area by cutting and rearranging pieces.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.4 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe a set of parallelograms (a)–(g) on the same base between the same parallel lines. (i) What can we say about the areas of all these parallelograms? (ii) What can we say about their perimeters? Which has maximum/minimum perimeter?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.4 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the areas of four parallelograms with dimensions: (i) base 7 cm, height 3 cm; (ii) base 5 cm, height 4 cm; (iii) base 4.8 cm, height 5 cm; (iv) base 4.4 cm, height 2 cm.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.4 p.163
homework.description: A rectangle and a parallelogram have the same side-lengths: 5 cm and 4 cm. Which has the greater area? Justify using the dissection or height argument.

time_bands.activity: Activity (parallelogram dissection), section 7.4 p.161 (“Using a cut-out of a parallelogram, convert it into a rectangle of equal area…”): each student cuts a paper parallelogram, slides the triangular piece to the opposite end, and assembles a rectangle. The class names the congruence justification — RHS — for the two triangles.

Figure it Out Q1, section 7.4 p.162 (“Observe a set of parallelograms (a)–(g) on the same base between the same parallel lines…”): students reason that all parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels share the same height, hence the same area, but their perimeters differ.

Figure it Out Q2, section 7.4 p.163 (“Find the areas of four parallelograms…”): students apply the formula area = base × height to all four cases, reinforcing that the slant side is irrelevant to area.

The teacher derives the formula a second time using the other pair of parallel sides, showing that the same parallelogram can be measured from either base with its corresponding height, and that both give the same area. Students verify numerically with one example from Q2.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error is using the slant side instead of the perpendicular height; having students physically measure the height of their cut-out rectangle (not the original slant edge) makes this concrete. The RHS congruence step — right angle, equal hypotenuse, equal side — should be articulated explicitly as it connects dissection proof to the formal deductive apparatus students know from triangle congruence.
materials: Paper parallelogram cut-outs (pre-drawn on plain paper by students)

periods.activity_title: From Diagonal to Diagonal Product: Deriving the Rhombus Area

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.4 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find QN in parallelogram PQRS given PQ = 7.6 cm, SM = 6 cm (altitude from S to PQ), and SR = 12 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (rhombus dissection), section 7.5 p.164
textbook_items_in_class.description: Work out how to convert a rhombus into a rectangle of equal area by dissecting the two isosceles triangles formed by one diagonal.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.6 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of a rhombus whose diagonals are 20 cm and 15 cm.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 7.4 p.164
homework.description: Which has greater area — an equilateral triangle or a square of the same side-length? Which has greater area — two identical equilateral triangles together or a square of the same side-length? Give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.4 p.163 (“Find QN in parallelogram PQRS given PQ = 7.6 cm, SM = 6 cm…”): students apply the equal-area principle — both base-height products equal the same area — to find the unknown altitude QN. This closes the parallelogram work before opening the rhombus.

Activity (rhombus dissection), section 7.5 p.164 (“Work out how to convert a rhombus into a rectangle of equal area…”): students fold or cut a rhombus along one diagonal, dissect each isosceles triangle into a half-rectangle, and assemble the two half-rectangles into rectangle WXYZ. They measure the sides and express them in terms of the diagonals.

The teacher guides the class to express the rectangle's dimensions — full diagonal AC and half diagonal BD/2 — and derive: area of rhombus = (1/2) × diagonal AC × diagonal BD. An alternative derivation using the two triangles ADB and CDB (with perpendicular diagonals as altitudes) confirms the same formula.

Figure it Out Q1, section 7.6 p.169 (“Find the area of a rhombus whose diagonals are 20 cm and 15 cm”): students apply the diagonal-product formula immediately to a numerical case, checking their answer using the base × height route as a verification.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes apply the diagonal-product formula to non-rhombus parallelograms — clarify that it holds only when the diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other. Having built the rectangle WXYZ from the dissection makes the formula visual rather than abstract; students who missed the construction step should be asked to describe in words what WXYZ's sides represent before substituting numbers.
materials: Paper rhombus cut-outs (pre-drawn by students on plain paper)

periods.activity_title: Three Paths to One Formula: Deriving the Trapezium Area

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.6 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give a method to convert a rectangle into a rhombus of equal area using dissection.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3(i), section 7.6 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 ft and 18 ft and height 8 ft (composite figure with rectangular and triangular parts).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3(ii), section 7.6 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 24 m and 36 m and height 14 m.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3(iii), section 7.6 p.169
homework.description: Find the area of a composite figure with parallel sides 14 in and 18 ft and heights 12 ft and 8 ft.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.6 p.169 (“Give a method to convert a rectangle into a rhombus of equal area using dissection”): students reason in reverse — from rectangle to rhombus — briefly consolidating the rhombus dissection before pivoting to the trapezium.

The teacher presents the algebraic decomposition of trapezium WXYZ into a rectangle and two right triangles, assigns variables x, h, a, y to the relevant lengths, and guides students to sum the three areas: (1/2)h(x + y + 2a). Substituting b = x + y + a simplifies this to (1/2)h(a + b). Students annotate their own diagram as the derivation proceeds.

The teacher shows the two-copy verification: rotating a second congruent trapezium and joining it along a shared side produces a parallelogram of base (a + b) and height h, so each trapezium is half, confirming (1/2)h(a + b). Students record this as a second derivation.

Figure it Out Q3(i), section 7.6 p.169 (“Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 ft and 18 ft and height 8 ft…”) and Figure it Out Q3(ii), section 7.6 p.169 (“Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 24 m and 36 m and height 14 m”): students apply the formula to both numerical cases, checking units.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the slant leg of the trapezium with the height — stress that h is the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides. The two-copy-and-join derivation is particularly memorable; having students physically rotate a second cut-out and align it makes the parallelogram appear visibly.

periods.activity_title: Trapezium to Rectangle: Śulba-Sūtra Transformations and Composite Figures

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.6 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to convert an isosceles trapezium to a rectangle using dissection.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 7.6 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: A regular hexagon is divided into a trapezium, an equilateral triangle, and a rhombus. Find the ratio of their areas.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 7.6 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY. Show that the area of trapezium ZYXW equals the area of triangle ZWB (where B is a specific point on the construction).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.6 p.169
homework.description: Given trapezium ABCD and rectangle EFGH of equal area, find the vertices of the rectangle given that triangles AHI ≅ DGI and BEJ ≅ CFJ.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.6 p.169 (“[Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to convert an isosceles trapezium to a rectangle using dissection”): students cut a paper isosceles trapezium, locate the midpoint of a non-parallel side, and reassemble the two pieces into a rectangle. They verify the rectangle's dimensions equal the average of the parallel sides times the height.

Figure it Out Q7, section 7.6 p.170 (“A regular hexagon is divided into a trapezium, an equilateral triangle, and a rhombus…”): students identify the three regions in a regular hexagon, assign side-length s, express each region's area using the formulas derived, and find the three-way area ratio.

Figure it Out Q8, section 7.6 p.170 (“ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY. Show that…”): students construct the point B and write a deductive argument showing that the trapezium and triangle ZWB have equal area, using the midpoint and equal-area lemma for triangles on parallel lines.

periods.teacher_notes: The hexagon problem requires students to use the parallelogram formula, the rhombus formula, and the triangle formula in concert — watch for those who compute only one region and stop. For Q8, the equal-area argument depends on the midpoint lemma established in the triangle section; students who struggle should be prompted to express the trapezium area in terms of the two parallel sides and then show the triangle has the same expression.
materials: Paper isosceles trapezium cut-outs (drawn by students)

periods.activity_title: From Inches to Acres: Area Units in the Real World

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.7 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Unit conversion exercises: (i) express 5 in and 7.4 in in centimetres; (ii) express 5.08 cm and 11.43 cm in inches; (iii) find how many cm² is 1 in²; (iv) convert 161.29 cm² to in²; (v) find how many in² is 1 ft².

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the key conversion facts: 1 in = 2.54 cm, so 1 in² = 6.4516 cm²; 1 ft = 12 in; 1 acre = 43,560 ft²; 1 km² = 1,000,000 m². Students record these and derive 1 ft² = 144 in² as a quick check.

Figure it Out, section 7.7 p.170 (“Unit conversion exercises: (i) express 5 in and 7.4 in in centimetres…”): students work through all five parts, converting between inches and centimetres both for linear and area quantities, and identify the squaring effect on conversion factors.

Students estimate the area of an A4 sheet in cm² and then convert to in², comparing the estimate with the standard value. The class then estimates the area of the classroom in m², discusses how many classrooms would fit in a hectare, and checks with the acre-to-m² conversion.

The teacher introduces local Indian area units — bigha, gaj, katha, dhur, cent, ankanam — and the class discusses why different units persist across regions. Students convert one local unit of their choice (researching or using a teacher-given value) into m² and compare it to familiar spaces.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in area conversion is forgetting to square the linear conversion factor — students multiply by 2.54 instead of squaring it; a quick dimensional check (cm × cm vs in × in) resolves the confusion. The local-units discussion is purposely open-ended: the goal is awareness that area measurement is culturally situated, not a uniform global standard.

periods.activity_title: Formula Sprint: Mixed Area Problems Across All Shapes

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3(iv), section 7.6 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 in and a base and height 6 in.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk Q6, section 7.6 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the trapezium-to-rectangle conversion idea, construct a trapezium of area 144 cm².

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.4 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give a method to obtain a rectangle whose area is twice that of a given triangle. Think of different methods.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.2 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a triangle into a rectangle of equal area.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q3(iv), section 7.6 p.169 (“Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 in and a base and height 6 in”) and Math Talk Q6, section 7.6 p.170 (“Using the trapezium-to-rectangle conversion idea, construct a trapezium of area 144 cm²”): students work the numerical item, then invert the formula to construct a trapezium of prescribed area — applying the formula in both directions.

Figure it Out Q5, section 7.4 p.163 (“Give a method to obtain a rectangle whose area is twice that of a given triangle…”): groups devise multiple methods — using the enclosing rectangle, using the dissection argument — and present one method each. The class compares the approaches.

Figure it Out Q5, section 7.2 p.158 (“[Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a triangle into a rectangle of equal area”): students apply the dissection knowledge built across the chapter to write a step-by-step procedure, connecting the Śulba-Sūtra tradition to the dissection methods practised throughout.

Whole-class reflection: the teacher asks students to name, from memory, the area formula for each shape covered and the one dissection step that connects each to the rectangle. Volunteers state each formula and the class confirms or corrects.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who express the rectangle-from-triangle method using only the specific numbers in their sketch rather than a general procedure — prompt them to rewrite their method without using any particular measurement. The closing formula-recall activity is a low-stakes verbal check, not a test; accept partial responses and build on them collectively.

items.prompt: A rectangle has an area of 36 cm² and one side measuring 4 cm. What is the length of the other side?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9 cm, because area = length × width, so length = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the rectangle area formula in reverse: unknown side = area ÷ known side.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracted 4 from 36 instead of dividing, confusing area with perimeter-style arithmetic.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student assumed the rectangle is a square and both sides equal 4 cm, ignoring the given area.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied 36 by 4 instead of dividing, reversing the operation needed.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the rectangle area formula and try substituting the known values before solving.
inclusivity.challenge: Write one more example of your own where the area and one side are given, then swap with a partner to solve.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
exercise.description: Identify the missing side-lengths of composite rectangular figures given their areas: (i) an L-shaped figure with partial lengths 4 in, 3 in, 7 in, 2 in and areas 28 in² and 21 in²; (ii) a rectangle with one side 4 m, one side 11 m, and total area 50 m².

items.prompt: Two rectangles each have a perimeter of 24 cm. Rectangle P has dimensions 10 cm × 2 cm and Rectangle Q has dimensions 6 cm × 6 cm. Which has the greater area, and by how much? Explain why equal perimeters do not guarantee equal areas.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangle P has area 20 cm² and Rectangle Q has area 36 cm². Rectangle Q has the greater area by 16 cm². Equal perimeters do not guarantee equal areas because the product length × width changes even when 2(length + width) stays constant — distributing the perimeter more evenly (closer to a square) increases the area.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute each area using length × width, compare, and invoke the independence of perimeter and area.

inclusivity.support: Try computing each area step by step using the formula, then talk through with a partner why the results differ.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one dimension and find a third rectangle with perimeter 24 cm whose area lies between 20 cm² and 36 cm²; explain the pattern.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.151
exercise.description: A shaded path is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a larger rectangle ABCD. (i) Assign measurements of your choice and find the area of the path; give a formula. (ii) If the path width along each side is given, find its area by breaking into rectangles; give a formula. (iii) Determine whether the path area changes when the outer rectangle is shifted while keeping EFGH inside.

items.prompt: A triangle has base BC and apex X. Explain, using the enclosing-rectangle argument, why the area of the triangle is always (1/2) × base × height, regardless of whether the triangle is acute or obtuse. Your explanation should address both cases.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: For an acute triangle: draw the enclosing rectangle with the same base BC and height equal to the altitude from X. The diagonal of this rectangle splits it into two congruent right triangles, so the original triangle is exactly half the rectangle, giving area = (1/2) × base × height. For an obtuse triangle: the altitude from X falls outside BC. The triangle's area equals the area of the large right triangle (base extended to the foot of the altitude) minus the small right triangle outside BC. Both right triangles use the same height h, so the subtraction yields (1/2) × h × (extended base) − (1/2) × h × (extension) = (1/2) × h × BC, confirming the formula holds universally.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the enclosing-rectangle dissection for the acute case and the difference-of-two-right-triangles argument for the obtuse case.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the enclosing rectangle for the acute case first, then talk through your reasoning with a partner before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Now suppose the apex X is at the midpoint of the top edge of the enclosing rectangle — what fraction of the rectangle is the triangle? Does your argument still hold if the base is changed to a different side?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.157
exercise.description: Find the areas of three triangles: (i) triangle with base 4 cm and height 3 cm; (ii) triangle ENT with base EN = 4 cm and height 3.2 cm; (iii) triangle ANT with base AT = 3 cm and height from N.

items.prompt: Parallelogram ABCD has base AB = 8 cm and height (perpendicular distance between the parallel sides) h = 5 cm. A second parallelogram PQRS has the same base and the same perpendicular height but its slant side PQ is longer than AB. Which parallelogram has the greater area? Justify your answer using the dissection argument.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both parallelograms have the same area of 40 cm². The dissection argument shows that any parallelogram can be cut into a right triangle and a trapezoid that reassemble into a rectangle of dimensions base × height. Since both parallelograms share the same base (8 cm) and the same perpendicular height (5 cm), they produce the same rectangle, so their areas are equal. The slant side length is irrelevant to area.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the dissection proof: area = base × perpendicular height, independent of the slant side length.

inclusivity.support: Draw the two parallelograms side by side and mark the perpendicular height on each before comparing.
inclusivity.challenge: Suppose the slant side PQ is doubled in length while keeping base and height the same — what happens to the perimeter and the area? Generalise.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.4 p.162
exercise.description: Observe a set of parallelograms (a)–(g) on the same base between the same parallel lines. (i) What can we say about the areas of all these parallelograms? (ii) What can we say about their perimeters? Which has maximum/minimum perimeter?

items.prompt: A rhombus has diagonals of length 12 cm and 16 cm. Using the dissection argument that converts the rhombus into a rectangle, show that its area is (1/2) × 12 × 16 and state the dimensions of the rectangle formed.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The dissection splits the rhombus along one diagonal (say, length 12 cm) into two congruent isosceles triangles. Each triangle is then rearranged into a half-rectangle. The two half-rectangles join to form rectangle WXYZ whose sides are the full diagonal AC = 12 cm and half the other diagonal BD/2 = 8 cm. Area of rectangle = 12 × 8 = 96 cm². Since the rhombus equals the rectangle in area, area of rhombus = 96 cm² = (1/2) × 12 × 16.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Dissect the rhombus along one diagonal into two isosceles triangles, convert each into a half-rectangle, and join them to form a rectangle of dimensions d₁ × (d₂/2).

inclusivity.support: Sketch the rhombus, draw one diagonal, and label each half-diagonal before describing the dissection.
inclusivity.challenge: Verify the same answer using the two-triangle method: each triangle ADB and CDB has base d₂ and height d₁/2; confirm both routes give 96 cm².

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.6 p.169
exercise.description: Find the area of a rhombus whose diagonals are 20 cm and 15 cm.

items.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides of lengths a = 7 cm and b = 13 cm, and perpendicular height h = 6 cm. Using the two-congruent-copy derivation, show that the area of the trapezium equals (1/2) × h × (a + b) and compute the numerical answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Take a second congruent copy of the trapezium and rotate it 180°. Join the two copies along the side of length b to form a parallelogram. The parallelogram has base (a + b) and height h, so its area is h(a + b). Since the trapezium is exactly half the parallelogram, its area = (1/2) × h × (a + b) = (1/2) × 6 × (7 + 13) = (1/2) × 6 × 20 = 60 cm².
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rotate a congruent copy and join along a parallel side to form a parallelogram of base (a + b) and height h; the trapezium is half.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the two copies of the trapezium side by side, then describe in words what shape they form together before writing the formula.
inclusivity.challenge: Suppose you keep a + b = 20 cm and h = 6 cm but change the individual values of a and b. Does the area change? Explain why or why not.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.6 p.169
exercise.description: Give a method to convert a rectangle into a rhombus of equal area using dissection.

items.prompt: Trapezium ABCD has parallel sides AB = 10 cm and CD = 6 cm, and height 4 cm. A student claims the area is (10 + 6) × 4 = 64 cm². Identify the error and state the correct area.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student forgot to multiply by (1/2). The correct formula is area = (1/2) × height × (sum of parallel sides) = (1/2) × 4 × (10 + 6) = (1/2) × 4 × 16 = 32 cm². The error is applying the parallelogram formula (base × height) to a shape that is only half the corresponding parallelogram.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the trapezium area formula: (1/2) × h × (a + b), recognising that the trapezium is half the parallelogram formed by two congruent copies.

inclusivity.support: Write out the trapezium formula from the two-copy derivation before substituting the values.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a different trapezium (different a, b, h) that has the same area of 32 cm², and verify using the formula.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3(i), section 7.6 p.169
exercise.description: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 ft and 18 ft and height 8 ft (composite figure with rectangular and triangular parts).

items.prompt: Describe, step by step, how to convert an isosceles trapezium into a rectangle of equal area using a single straight cut, and explain why the two pieces produce a rectangle whose width equals the average of the two parallel sides.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Locate the midpoint M of one non-parallel (leg) side. Step 2: Make a horizontal cut through M parallel to the two parallel sides, producing a small triangle at the top and a larger trapezoid at the bottom. Step 3: Flip the small triangle and attach it to the opposite end. The result is a rectangle. The rectangle's width equals the average of the two parallel sides because the cut shifts half the difference between the longer and shorter parallel sides from one end to the other, making both ends equal in length, and that common length is (a + b)/2. The height of the rectangle equals the height of the original trapezium.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Cut horizontally through the midpoint of a leg, flip the top triangle to the opposite end, and use the average-of-parallel-sides interpretation to justify the rectangle's width.

inclusivity.support: Fold a paper cut-out of the trapezium to find the midpoint and physically make the cut, then assemble the rectangle.
inclusivity.challenge: Will the same method work for a non-isosceles trapezium? Explain whether the cut still produces a rectangle or a different shape.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.6 p.169
exercise.description: [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to convert an isosceles trapezium to a rectangle using dissection.

items.prompt: In triangle PQR, the base QR = 10 cm and the altitude from P to QR is 7 cm. A second altitude from Q meets PR at point S. If PR = 14 cm, find the length of altitude QS.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Area of triangle PQR = (1/2) × QR × (altitude from P) = (1/2) × 10 × 7 = 35 cm². Using the same area with base PR: 35 = (1/2) × PR × QS = (1/2) × 14 × QS, so QS = 70 ÷ 14 = 5 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Equate the two area expressions — (1/2) × base₁ × height₁ = (1/2) × base₂ × height₂ — and solve for the unknown altitude.

inclusivity.support: Draw the triangle and mark both altitudes; write the area using the known base and height first, then set it equal to the expression using the second base.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the third altitude from R to PQ if PQ = 17.5 cm, using the same area.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 7.2 p.158
exercise.description: ABCD, BCEF, and BFGH are three identical squares. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, find the area of the blue region. (ii) If the total area of blue and red regions is 180 sq. units, find the area of each square.

items.prompt: Quadrilateral KLMN has diagonal KM = 18 cm. The perpendicular distance from L to KM is 4 cm, and the perpendicular distance from N to KM is 6 cm. Find the area of quadrilateral KLMN.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Diagonal KM divides KLMN into two triangles: triangle KLM and triangle KNM, both with base KM = 18 cm. Area of triangle KLM = (1/2) × 18 × 4 = 36 cm². Area of triangle KNM = (1/2) × 18 × 6 = 54 cm². Total area of KLMN = 36 + 54 = 90 cm².
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose the quadrilateral into two triangles using the diagonal, compute each triangle's area, and sum.

inclusivity.support: Draw the quadrilateral and its diagonal first; label the two triangles before computing either area.
inclusivity.challenge: If the two perpendicular distances were equal (both equal to 5 cm) but the diagonal stayed 18 cm, what would the area be? What kind of quadrilateral would produce equal perpendicular distances from opposite vertices to a diagonal?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.160
exercise.description: Find the area of quadrilateral ABCD given AC = 22 cm, BM ⊥ AC with BM = 3 cm, and DN ⊥ AC with DN = 3 cm.

items.prompt: A rectangular notice board measures 2 ft by 1.5 ft. (i) Find its area in square inches. (ii) Convert that area to square centimetres. (Use: 1 ft = 12 in; 1 in = 2.54 cm.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (i) Convert dimensions: 2 ft = 24 in; 1.5 ft = 18 in. Area = 24 × 18 = 432 in². (ii) 1 in = 2.54 cm, so 1 in² = 2.54² = 6.4516 cm². Area = 432 × 6.4516 ≈ 2787.09 cm².
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert linear dimensions to inches first, compute area in in², then multiply by 6.4516 (the squared linear conversion factor) to get cm².

inclusivity.support: Convert each dimension from feet to inches separately using 1 ft = 12 in, then find the area before tackling the centimetre conversion.
inclusivity.challenge: Now convert the area to m² and estimate how many such notice boards would cover exactly 1 m².

exercise.description: Unit conversion exercises: (i) express 5 in and 7.4 in in centimetres; (ii) express 5.08 cm and 11.43 cm in inches; (iii) find how many cm² is 1 in²; (iv) convert 161.29 cm² to in²; (v) find how many in² is 1 ft².

items.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides of 9 in and 5 in, and a perpendicular height of 8 in. Find its area in square inches.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Area = (1/2) × height × (sum of parallel sides) = (1/2) × 8 × (9 + 5) = (1/2) × 8 × 14 = 56 in².
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the trapezium area formula: (1/2) × h × (a + b).

inclusivity.support: Write out the trapezium formula first, then substitute the three given values one at a time.
inclusivity.challenge: Keep the area at 56 in² but change the height to 7 in; find a new pair of parallel sides a and b whose sum satisfies the formula, with a ≠ b.
